nameStory: The Little Gull earned its straightforward name by being the smallest gull species in the entire world! At roughly the size of a robin, this petite seabird makes other gulls look like giants in comparison. The scientific name Hydrocoloeus means 'water dweller,' perfectly capturing this bird's love of both freshwater lakes and ocean waters.
description: The Little Gull is a tiny, delicate seabird that's much smaller than the familiar gulls you see at the beach. About the size of a robin, it has a compact body with relatively narrow, pointed wings that give it a tern-like appearance in flight. During breeding season, adults develop a distinctive black hood, while in winter they show just a dark cap and ear spot. This rare visitor to New England is most often spotted along the coast during migration or winter months.

idTips.label: Tiny Size
idTips.description: Noticeably smaller than any other gull - about robin-sized with a delicate, almost fragile appearance that makes nearby gulls look massive

idTips.label: Dark Wing Undersides
idTips.description: In flight, look for distinctive dark gray to blackish undersides of the wings, creating a striking contrast with the white body

idTips.label: Rounded Head
idTips.description: Small, round head that appears proportionally large for the body, giving it an almost dove-like profile

idTips.label: Tern-like Flight
idTips.description: Flies with quick, fluttery wingbeats more like a tern than the steady, powerful flight of larger gulls

idTips.label: Black Hood or Cap
idTips.description: Breeding adults show a complete black hood, while non-breeding birds have a dark cap and distinctive dark ear spot

idTips.label: Thin Bill
idTips.description: Small, thin, dark bill that's much more delicate than the chunky bills of larger gulls

habitat: Little Gulls are most often found along New England's coastline, particularly in harbors, estuaries, and nearshore ocean waters during migration and winter. They occasionally appear at large inland lakes and reservoirs, especially during stormy weather when they may be blown inland. Look for them mixed in with flocks of other gulls and terns, often feeding over deeper water rather than scavenging on beaches.

seasonality.spring: Rare spring migrants may appear from March through May, usually in breeding plumage with distinctive black hoods. Most sightings occur during stormy weather or at major birding locations along the coast.
seasonality.summer: Very uncommon in summer, with only occasional non-breeding individuals spotted along the coast. Any summer sightings are noteworthy and should be documented carefully.
seasonality.fall: Peak migration time from September through November, when most New England sightings occur. Birds may be in various stages of molt, showing mixed breeding and non-breeding plumage features.
seasonality.winter: Small numbers may winter along the coast, particularly in harbors and sheltered bays. Winter birds show clean white heads with dark caps and ear spots.

funFact: Little Gulls are such recent colonizers of North America that the first confirmed breeding didn't occur until 1962 in Ontario, and they've only been regularly spotted in New England since the 1970s - making every sighting a piece of ongoing natural history!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with Bonaparte's Gull, but Little Gull is noticeably smaller with darker wing undersides and a more delicate build. Remember: Little Gull = little size, dark wing linings; Bonaparte's Gull = bigger body, white wing linings underneath.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'gull,' Little Gulls behave more like terns, often picking food delicately from the water's surface rather than scavenging like typical gulls. They're also the only species in their genus, making them quite unique in the gull family tree.
compareHints: As the only species in its genus, Little Gull is most similar to Bonaparte's Gull in the genus Chroicocephalus. However, Little Gull is significantly smaller, has darker wing undersides in flight, and shows more delicate proportions overall. Bonaparte's Gull is chunkier with bright white wing undersides and a thicker, more typical gull-like bill.
